newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Smoker sues France's Seita over cancer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Smoker sues France's Seita over cancer.

text.p: A two-pack-a-day smoker is suing French tobacco giant Seita for 2.3 million francs ($437,400), accusing the company of causing his cancer in the first legal case of its kind ever brought in France, Seita said on Thursday.
Seita, which has a national monopoly on tobacco products distribution, said the smoker "attributes his cancer to his consumption" of its famed pungent Gauloises Brunes cigarettes.

The smoker, Richard Gourlain, and his relatives "are claiming damages for the harm they believe they have suffered citing a lack of information about the dangers of tobacco consumption," Seita said in a statement.
A Seita spokeswoman called the allegations unfounded and said the company was "absolutely confident" about the outcome of the case filed in a suburban Paris district court.

After the suit against Seita was announced, its shares dropped nearly one percent before retracing most of their losses. By early afternoon, the stock was down 0.28 percent at 212.20 francs against an overall stronger share market.

The French newspaper Le Parisien said Gourlain suffered tongue and lung cancer and had smoked for 30 years. It said he had lost his job because of the illness, which had reduced him to a shell of a man weighing just 49 kilos.
It quoted his wife as saying the "little blue (Gauloise) packets had ruined her life".
The company's flagship Gauloises and Gitanes dark tobacco cigarettes were trademarks of Gallic chic for generations but demand has waned in recent years in favour of lighter brands.
While the number of cigarette smokers in France has fallen slightly, it is estimated that some 40 percent of men and nearly 30 percent of women still smoke.

Seita, privatised last year, said the only similar legal proceedings ever filed in France were brought against a bank by the family of an employee who claimed she was the victim of passive smoking. That case was thrown out by a Paris district court on lack of sufficient legal proof.
French cigarettes started carrying warning notices about the health effects of smoking in 1976 and tobacco advertising now is banned.
The case comes on the heels of a number of high-profile cases brought in the United States against U.S. tobacco companies.

Earlier this year, the industry was badly jolted when a Jacksonville, Florida jury awarded $750,000 to lung cancer sufferer Grady Carter, who argued that Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp misled him into believing smoking was safe. The tobacco company is appealing the verdict.

In Florida, a landmark class action suit has been launched by a doctor who claims he became sick from smoking. As many as 500,000 Florida smokers could be eligible to join the lawsuit. ($1=5.258 French Franc)
